parts.title: A year in Canada
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When I was fifteen, I spent a school year in Canada, and it was the hardest and the best year of my life. Before I left Spain, I thought my English was quite good. I had always had high marks at school, and I could understand the songs I listened to. Then I arrived at the airport in Vancouver, and a woman at the desk asked me a question that I did not understand at all.

My host family was very patient. They spoke slowly, and they used a lot of gestures. During the first month, I was so tired in the evenings that I fell asleep as soon as I came home. Listening all day to a foreign language is very hard work. I often smiled and nodded without knowing what people had said, and once I agreed to eat something that turned out to be a very hot chilli.

The change came slowly. One morning, I realised that I had been thinking in English for an hour without noticing. A few weeks later, I made my first joke in English, and my host sister laughed. It was one of the proudest moments of my life.

At the end of the year, I could talk to anybody about almost anything. I also had friends from five different countries. I learned that you need to make mistakes if you want to improve. People did not mind when I used the wrong word, and they usually helped me to find the right one. When I came home, I missed Canada so much that I started to write my diary in English, and I still do.

parts.title: Growing up with two languages
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Do you know that more than half of the people in the world speak at least two languages? [1] In many countries, children grow up with two or three languages at home, and they move easily from one to the other.

Scientists have studied bilingual children for many years. [2] For example, they can often concentrate better, and they find it easier to learn a third language later.

However, being bilingual is not always simple. Some children mix words from both languages in one sentence, and parents sometimes worry. [3] Teachers say that this is normal, and that it usually stops as the child gets older.

Families who want to raise bilingual children have several options. One common method is that each parent speaks a different language to the child. [4] Others speak one language at home and the other one outside the house.

Whatever method they choose, experts agree on one thing: children need plenty of chances to hear and use both languages. [5] A grandparent who tells stories in the second language can be just as helpful as an expensive school.
sentences: Some families also ask a relative to talk to the child in a different language.
It does not always have to be a formal lesson, as this can be done through games, songs and conversation.
They found that these children often have some advantages at school.
Hundreds of different languages are spoken in big cities such as London.
In fact, this is a normal stage of learning two languages at the same time.
Being bilingual is therefore normal for a large part of the population.

gaps.explanation: The question about half the world speaking two languages is answered by sentence F: being bilingual is normal; the next sentence is about children growing up with languages.
"Scientists have studied bilingual children" leads to what they found; "For example" gives the advantages.
Parents worry about mixed words; "In fact, this is a normal stage" reassures them, and the next sentence says teachers agree.
One method is each parent using a different language; "Others speak..." in the next sentence is a second method, and sentence A is another option that fits between them.
Children need chances to hear both languages; the next sentence says it does not have to be formal, and the final sentence gives the example of a grandparent.

parts.title: Learning new words
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Many students believe that the best way to learn vocabulary is to read a long list and try to [1] it by heart. Unfortunately, this method does not usually work. Research shows that we remember words better when we meet them several times in different [2]. One idea is to keep a small notebook. Each time you hear a new word, write it down with an example sentence and a picture. Another helpful idea is to review your notes [3] a day or two later, and again after a week. You will then be more [4] to remember the word for a long time. You can also stick small notes with words onto the objects in your room. Every time you look at the door or the window, you will see its name, and the word will gradually become [5] of your memory. Finally, do not be afraid to use new words, even if you [6] a mistake.

questions.prompt: Gap 2

questions.prompt: Gap 3

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: "More likely to remember" means there is a better chance of remembering.

parts.title: An email to a host family
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Dear Mr and Mrs Rowe,
Thank you very much for agreeing to have me in your house [1] the summer. I am looking forward to meeting you all. My English is not perfect, [2] I will try to speak as much as I can. I am arriving at the airport on Saturday [3] two o'clock. I will wear a blue jacket, so you [4] recognise me easily. I have never been to England, so I do not know [5] the weather will be like. Should I bring a raincoat? Please tell me if there is anything that I [6] not eat.
Best wishes,
Marta

gaps.explanation: "For the summer" says how long she will stay.
"But" contrasts her imperfect English with her promise to try.
We use "at" with a clock time.
A modal verb says that they will be able to recognise her.
"What the weather will be like" is the correct indirect question.
"Anything I must not eat" refers to foods that she should avoid.

parts.title: An interview with a Spanish teacher
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Augustina, you teach Spanish to adults in the evenings. Did you always want to be a teacher?

turns.speaker: augustina
turns.text: Not at all. I studied history at university, and I only began to learn languages because I wanted to read old letters. A friend then told me about a teaching course, and I loved it from the first day.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How many languages do you speak?

turns.speaker: augustina
turns.text: Four fluently, and I can get by in two more. But that's not the point. A good teacher is not someone who knows a lot of words. It's someone who helps people to understand each other.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the hardest thing about the job?

turns.speaker: augustina
turns.text: Patience. Adult students are often shy, and they are afraid of making mistakes. It can take months before they speak without worrying. I try to make the classroom a friendly place, and we laugh a lot.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Have you ever made a funny mistake yourself?

turns.speaker: augustina
turns.text: Once, in a class about food, I wrote the word for 'cow' on the board when I meant 'cold'. Everybody looked confused, and then a student started to laugh. After that, I always checked my words before a lesson.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Will computers replace teachers?

turns.speaker: augustina
turns.text: Computers are getting better, but they cannot understand jokes, or feelings, or what is not said. People still prefer to learn with a human being, especially when they are nervous.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What advice do you give to young people?

turns.speaker: augustina
turns.text: Spend time where your language is spoken, even for a short time. Books will teach you grammar, but only life will teach you how people really talk.
